reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Rare pulmonary vascular disease classified within WHO Group 1 prime alongside pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (PVOD), with which it shares clinical, genetic and histological overlap along a disease continuum.
Biallelic (recessive) loss-of-function mutations in EIF2AK4 (encoding GCN2) underlie heritable forms and are shared with PVOD, supporting the view that the two are variants of one entity.
Histology shows proliferation of thin-walled capillaries infiltrating alveolar septa, bronchovascular bundles, pleura and the walls of pulmonary veins and arteries.
Presents like idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (progressive exertional dyspnoea, right heart failure) but with a disproportionately low DLCO and marked hypoxaemia.
Haemoptysis and occult alveolar haemorrhage (haemosiderin-laden macrophages on lavage) are clues that help separate it from idiopathic PAH.
HRCT typically shows diffuse or centrilobular ground-glass nodules, smooth interlobular septal thickening and mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
Life-threatening pulmonary oedema may be precipitated by PAH-targeted vasodilators, especially prostacyclins, a hallmark shared with PVOD.
Lung transplantation is the only definitive therapy, so early referral to a transplant centre is essential.
reference.pathophysiology: PCH is characterised by abnormal proliferation of pulmonary capillaries that invade and infiltrate the alveolar interstitium and, importantly, the walls of pulmonary veins and arteries as well as the pleura and airways. Capillary infiltration and obstruction at and beyond the post-capillary level produce venous congestion and pulmonary hypertension with a venous-obstructive component, explaining the overlap with PVOD. Biallelic EIF2AK4 mutations impair the integrated stress response and are thought to predispose to dysregulated angioproliferation. The remodelled capillary bed raises pulmonary vascular resistance, and because the obstruction lies at or beyond the capillary level, potent arterial vasodilators can flood an unprotected downstream bed and precipitate acute pulmonary oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis or other diffuse interstitial lung disease
Lymphangitis carcinomatosa or metastatic pulmonary calcinosis
additionalInvestigations: Right heart catheterisation (wedge pressure often normal despite venous congestion)
Full pulmonary function testing with DLCO (markedly reduced)
Surgical lung biopsy (rarely performed owing to bleeding risk; diagnosis is often clinico-radiological)
redFlags: Acute pulmonary oedema after starting PAH-targeted vasodilators
Decompensated right heart failure with syncope or hypotension
reference.prognosis: The course is progressive and generally poor, with median survival of only a few years from diagnosis without transplantation. Lung transplantation is potentially curative and offers the best long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as idiopathic PAH leading to aggressive vasodilator therapy and fatal pulmonary oedema.
Attributing the low DLCO and ground-glass changes to interstitial lung disease rather than a pulmonary vascular cause.
Delaying transplant referral because pulmonary pressures initially appear to respond to therapy.
Assuming a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure excludes a post-capillary or venous component.
references: ERS/ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension
Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Early referral for lung transplantation, the only potentially curative treatment, given the progressive course
Avoid, or use only under expert supervision, targeted pulmonary vasodilators, as they can flood the unprotected distal bed and precipitate fatal pulmonary oedema
Supportive management with diuretics for right heart failure and supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia
Use anticoagulation and any pulmonary hypertension-directed measures only with specialist guidance and close monitoring for pulmonary oedema
Genetic testing and counselling for biallelic EIF2AK4 mutations, with screening of at-risk relatives
Right heart catheterisation and serial haemodynamic and functional assessment to characterise and monitor the disease
Manage within a specialist pulmonary vascular and transplant centre
